items.name: primary-workload EKS cluster
items.description: Main EKS cluster: istio mesh, AWS Load Balancer Controller, CoreDNS, Karpenter, ~600 workloads across 10 namespaces.

replication.notes: Shape, not bytes: the cluster, its node pools and its add-ons are rebuilt from terraform/eks-setup and re-synced by GitOps. Nothing here is replicated, so there is no RPO — there is a build time. Test #2 measured ~40 min from apply to apps Ready, and that number dominates the RTA.

outboundCalls.failoverBehavior: explicit ARNs must exist in recovery region

verification.command: kubectl get nodes && kubectl get pods -n kube-system

items.notes: Layer correction: cmp_secrets (L3) was removed from dependsOn. The cluster (L2) does not need the secret store to exist — its WORKLOADS do, and each L4 workload declares cmp_secrets itself. Declaring it here made an L2 component depend on an L3 one, and the tool prints the layer order as the recovery order, so operators were told to wait for secrets before the cluster.

The pod starts and goes Ready without the partner; it is the L6 settlement success bar that needs the partner path, so the partner belongs at L5 as a verify-before-the-bar precondition, not as an L4 startup dependency. items.name: Aurora — adjudication
items.description: Claims system of record.

replication.notes: Aurora Global Database: us-east-1 primary, us-east-2 secondary, storage-level async replication. A planned switchover is RPO 0; an UNPLANNED failover loses whatever had not shipped — typically well under a second of writes. Quote the unplanned figure. 1 minute is recorded as a conservative ceiling; the number to put in a test record is the measured replica lag at T0 (AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag). Aurora PostgreSQL can enforce a ceiling with rds.global_db_rpo, which blocks commits when lag exceeds it.

verification.pass: connect + query OK from recovered app pod

items.notes: The secondary is kept small and is scaled up at failover — managed failover is "order of minutes", not seconds, and the scale-up is part of the RTA. Verify the secondary's instance class against full production load before trusting the number.

items.name: Aurora — pricing
items.description: Pricing reference data.

replication.notes: AWS Backup cross-region copy, daily. Deliberate: pricing reference data is reloaded from the drug-price feed on a weekly cycle, so the RPO here is the backup cadence (24 h) and a global cluster would buy nothing. Copies are re-encrypted with the destination vault key, so the recovery-region vault key has to exist first.

verification.pass: a copied recovery point for the pricing cluster dated within 24 h

items.notes: A store whose RPO is a day is a decision, not an oversight — it is written down here so nobody has to re-derive it during an event.

items.name: Aurora — remittance
items.description: Remittance/settlement records.

replication.notes: THIRD-PARTY: recovered from Arpio recovery points (snapshot-based point-in-time recovery), configured at 30 min. This is the one Tier-0 store still on point-in-time recovery rather than continuous replication, and it is the one that missed — test #2 measured a 118-min RPA against the 30-min configuration because the recovery points were not aligned across stores. Kept here on purpose as the contrast with cmp_aurora_adj: snapshot recovery gives you a consistent moment, not a current one. Migration to Aurora Global Database is the open item in dec_mechanisms.

verification.command: psql from a pod: SELECT now() - max(settled_at) FROM remittances
verification.pass: connects, and the age at T0 is recorded as the measured RPA

gaps: Measured RPA of 118 min against a 30-min configured recovery point — points were not aligned across stores (gap_rpa1)

items.name: Redis — adjudication cache
items.description: Adjudication cache; acceptable to rebuild cold.

replication.notes: Cache — rebuilt cold on failover. The number this owes the program is not an RPO, it is how much extra load the cold cache puts on Aurora at cutover; measure it in a test. ElastiCache Global Datastore is the alternative if that load turns out to be unacceptable.

items.name: Redis — pricing cache

replication.notes: Cache — rebuilt cold on failover. Note that AWS Backup does not cover ElastiCache at all, so "it is on backup" is not an available answer here: the choices are Global Datastore, ElastiCache's own snapshots with cross-region copy, or a deliberate cold start.

items.name: SQS — claim-stream queues
items.description: Claim processing queues. The queue is recreated in the recovery region; messages in flight at the recovery point are lost.

replication.notes: THIRD-PARTY: the queue and its configuration come back from an Arpio recovery point. Read this carefully, because it is the clearest shape-vs-bytes example in the workspace — no tool, vendor or AWS-native, moves SQS messages across regions. What the recovery point restores is the QUEUE; the in-flight messages are accepted loss, documented in the RPO statement. No rpoMinutes is recorded because the number that would matter has no mechanism behind it.

verification.pass: queue exists with the expected redrive policy and visibility timeout

gaps: In-flight message loss is accepted but has never been sized (max in-flight x processing lag)

items.name: SQS — payee queues
items.description: Remittance payee processing queues.

replication.notes: Same problem as cmp_sqs_claims, different answer: the queue is simply recreated by Terraform and the consumer is idempotent, re-driving from the remittance store as the source of truth. That is the pattern to prefer — it makes the queue rebuildable state and the RPO question disappears.

verification.pass: queue exists; consumer re-drive from the remittance store succeeds

items.name: S3 — stream/transfer/claim-report buckets
items.description: Claim reports, transfer staging, stream archives.

replication.notes: S3 Cross-Region Replication to the us-east-2 buckets. Most objects replicate in seconds, but WITHOUT Replication Time Control there is no upper bound at all — 15 min is recorded as a planning number, and turning RTC on is what converts it into a commitment (RTC design goal: 99.99% of objects within 15 min; the SLA credit line is 99.9%). CRR only replicates objects written after it was enabled.

verification.pass: object present; ReplicationStatus COMPLETED on the source object

gaps: Bucket names may be region-bound in app config — check before failover
Objects written before CRR was enabled were never backfilled — the S3 Batch Replication job has not been run

items.name: Secrets Manager (~50 explicit ARNs)
items.description: Runtime secrets consumed by secrets-init at pod start. The single most common cause of failed recovery tests.

replication.notes: Replica secrets in us-east-2. The replica keeps the SAME NAME (only the region in the ARN differs), so name-based lookup fails over cleanly, and rotation propagates to replicas automatically. Propagation is event-driven — 1 min is a conservative ceiling, not a lag budget. The failure mode here is not lag, it is list drift: a secret nobody marked for replication simply is not there, and every replica needs a KMS key in the recovery region to decrypt with. Three lists still disagree (replica-enabled secrets, the manual spreadsheet, the runtime logical names) — that is what killed test #2.

verification.command: secrets-init logs clean; every runtime logical name resolves
verification.pass: no ResourceNotFoundException on any logical name

gaps: Secret lists disagree — reconcile into one signed-off CSV of logical names, then verify each one is replicated

Edge/WAF reachability and the partner IP allowlist are L5 work (04-restore-layer-cake.md: 'partner allowlists/egress IPs confirmed'), and they are a PRECONDITION of the L7 DNS flip, not part of it. items.name: ECR — 17 repositories (ops account)
items.description: Container images the recovered pods pull from. Replicated continuously into the recovery region, so the images are already there — but the pull path is what an L4 failure blames an L1 cause for.

replication.notes: Native ECR cross-region replication rules at registry level; AWS states the majority of images replicate in under 30 min. Two traps: only images pushed AFTER the rule was created are replicated (the backlog has to be re-pushed), and repository settings and lifecycle policies are NOT replicated — recreate those with IaC. A pull-through cache rule needs an internet path on first pull, so pre-replicate rather than relying on it in an isolated drill.

verification.pass: image host is the recovery-region registry

items.notes: The registry is the first thing to prove: a pod that cannot pull is an L4 symptom with an L1 cause. Verify both that the repositories exist and that a pod-identity pull actually succeeds.

items.notes: Layer correction: L6 -> L5, per 14-third-party-dependencies.md ('every third party is a component, usually layer L5') and 04-restore-layer-cake.md's own worked example ('the clearinghouse allowlist L5'). L6 is the functional success bar; a partner is a PRECONDITION of that bar. Scheduling partner/allowlist work at L6 means you discover an allowlist miss after the L5 gate has already passed — i.e. after the last point at which you could still have done something about it.
